evidence.title: Tibo Just Vowed "28 Consecutive Days of Model Releases or Resets"
evidence.body: [e003:f01] Tibo has posted yet again... [e003:f02] This time, he said OpenAI has "locked in its direction": going forward, it will only focus on four categories of work — simplifying products, improving efficiency to support more usage, delivering breakthrough features, and launching new models . [e003:f03] " Ahead of the Developers Day, OpenAI raised expectations extremely high, and users have heard too many similar remarks: 20 new features, major updates, about to change the way of working... [e003:f04] However, after the conference ended, many heavy users found that several problems that really affect the daily experience have not disappeared: the quota is reduced, the model runs slower, and the most anticipated new product does not immediately show the value promoted in the publicity. [e003:f05] One user directly said that before DevDay, OpenAI gave people the feeling that "this time everything will be changed", but after the actual release, " it is basically useless ". [e003:f06] The problem with OpenAI's Developers Day this time is precisely that there are a lot of releases, but few of them are retained in actual use. [e003:f07] Tibo even previewed in advance that about 20 new things would be announced, giving people the feeling that there would almost be a full product line refresh. [e003:f08] GPT-6.1 Sol, new Codex / Work capabilities, Dots, and a series of updates around Agent, developer tools and ChatGPT were launched one after another. [e003:f09] Judging only by the number of releases, it is hard to say this DevDay has "no real content". [e003:f10] In addition to the disappointment conveyed by Scott earlier, other users also gave similar evaluations. [e003:f11] OpenAI has previously adjusted subscriptions and usage quotas due to computing power pressure, and registration for new users of the $200 package was once suspended; later the usage quotas were significantly tightened. [e003:f12] At the same time, the official explanation emphasized more that "the efficiency of the model has been improved" and "the same quota can complete more work". [e003:f13] It is also under this background that the "simplification" goal proposed by Tibo may be more worthy of in-depth consideration. [e003:f14] Therefore, "becoming simpler" may be the right direction The direction OpenAI has locked in next is: simplifying products, improving efficiency to support more usage, delivering breakthrough features, and launching new models. [e003:f15] Users certainly want more powerful models, as well as new Agents and new ways of working. [e003:f16] In the next 28 days, let's see if the quality can catch up.

evidence.title: OpenAI and Anthropic use private capital to delay US IPOs amid yield spike
evidence.body: [e004:f01] OpenAI and Anthropic are leveraging substantial private funding to control their public market entry timelines, effectively bypassing the current freeze in the US initial public offering (IPO) market. [e004:f02] While rising 10-year Treasury yields exceeding 5% have forced issuers in consumer hardware, energy, and dining to postpone listings, these leading artificial intelligence developers retain the financial flexibility to defer debuts until conditions improve. ## Private capital buffers enable strategic delays Major AI firms are utilizing private capital rounds to fund high-cost infrastructure investments without the immediate pressure of public market scrutiny or unfavorable valuations. [e004:f03] OpenAI has ruled out a 2026 IPO, pushing its timeline to 2027, while Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November debut. [e004:f04] Luke Lango, technology analyst and editor of Innovation Investor, characterized OpenAI’s move as a deferral rather than a defection. [e004:f05] "Only the public markets are deep enough for both equity and the debt needed to build data centers... [e004:f06] That’s a luxury only the top two or three players have." Viram Shah, CEO of Vested, noted that OpenAI raised **$122 billion** in March and is seeking at least **$30 billion** more at a valuation of approximately **$1.4 trillion**. [e004:f07] However, Shah emphasized that at this scale, they will eventually require public markets for long-term capital and employee liquidity. ## Market conditions stalling broader listings The cooling IPO environment is driven by macroeconomic headwinds, particularly the surge in benchmark interest rates. [e004:f08] The US 10-year Treasury yield reached **5.29%** on September 29, 2026, marking a 19-year high following a Federal Reserve rate hike on September 16. [e004:f09] Consequently, seven sizable US IPOs were postponed or pulled in the third quarter of 2026, compared to four in the second quarter and three in the first quarter, according to Vested data. ## Valuation compression impacts non-AI sectors Companies outside the top-tier AI sector face greater pressure to list despite unfavorable terms. [e004:f10] Smart-ring maker Oura postponed its planned **$2.2 billion** US listing on September 29, citing market uncertainty. [e004:f11] The company reported **$61 million** in profit on **$1.2 billion** in sales across the first three quarters of its fiscal year, with expected full-year revenue growth of 90%. [e004:f12] Despite strong financials, investors raised concerns over its target valuation of approximately **$15.6 billion** and single-product exposure. [e004:f13] Nuclear services company Holtec International withdrew its US IPO filing, SoftBank-backed SB Energy delayed its listing following valuation pushback, and Inspire Brands deferred IPO consideration. ## What the numbers show The divergence between AI leaders and other tech firms highlights a concentration of capital access. [e004:f14] While Oura, with **$1.2 billion** in sales and positive profitability, was forced to withdraw due to valuation gaps, OpenAI’s ability to raise **$122 billion** privately insulates it from the same repricing pressures. [e004:f15] This suggests that in the current high-yield environment, only companies with massive private balance sheets can dictate their public debut timing, while mid-cap growth firms must either accept lower valuations or remain private longer. ## Conditions for reopening the IPO window Analysts identify specific benchmarks required to stabilize the market for broader listings: * **Treasury Yield Stabilization:** Yields need to stop spiking rather than fall significantly. [e004:f16] The 10-year yield rose 0.54 percentage points in September alone. * **Federal Reserve Policy Clarity:** A clear signal that the rate-hiking cycle is paused is essential for pricing deals with confidence. * **Hyperscaler Expenditure Metrics:** Late-October earnings from major cloud providers must confirm that AI capital expenditures are generating revenue. * **Aftermarket Performance:** Successful trading in upcoming listings, such as Anthropic’s potential November debut, could provide market confirmation.

OpenAI IPO Date: Investor Timeline, Valuation and Expectations
evidence.body: [e001:f01] OpenAI has been making noise with both its LLM and its potential IPO. [e001:f02] OpenAI has formally started the IPO process, but investors still don’t have an official OpenAI IPO date. [e001:f03] What We Know About OpenAI’s Current Status and IPO Plans OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015. [e001:f04] Bottom Line OpenAI confidentially submitted its S-1 on June 8, 2026, but it has not announced an official IPO date. [e001:f05] 2 That tension between rapid growth and extraordinary spending may ultimately matter more to investors than the exact IPO date. [e001:f06] Expected Valuation and What Investors Would Be Paying OpenAI’s valuation has risen far beyond the $80 billion level cited in earlier funding rounds. [e001:f07] In March 2026, OpenAI raised $122 billion at an $852 billion post-money valuation. [e001:f08] Using that figure, here’s what several hypothetical revenue multiples would imply: Revenue Multiple Implied Valuation 15x $600 billion 20x $800 billion 25x $1.0 trillion 30x $1.2 trillion These aren’t IPO price targets. [e001:f09] The remaining process could include SEC comments and revisions, publication of a registration statement, an investor roadshow, pricing, and finally the first day of trading. [e001:f10] Recent Financial Times reporting says OpenAI is considering another private funding round and that CEO Sam Altman has suggested an IPO likely won’t happen before 2027. [e001:f11] Falling technology valuations, weaker investor appetite for AI or greater regulatory uncertainty could delay an offering. [e001:f12] OpenAI, Anthropic and the AI IPO Market OpenAI won’t be valued in a vacuum. [e001:f13] It has also confidentially filed for an IPO and reached a $965 billion private valuation in May 2026. [e001:f14] But future investors will also want to understand OpenAI’s obligations to Microsoft, its reliance on outside computing providers, and how much flexibility it has to form competing partnerships. [e001:f15] The company’s growth could remain exceptional while its stock still disappoints if investors pay a valuation that assumes too much future success. [e001:f16] OpenAI’s revenue growth, losses, cash requirements and IPO valuation will show how much future AI dominance is already built into the price.

evidence.title: Can superintelligence ever be controlled? Sam Altman on AI safety, doomsday scenarios, and OpenAI's delayed IPO
evidence.body: [e002:f01] OpenAI’s CEO argues that humanity can remain in control of AI—if the industry puts safety ahead of speed, competition, and an imminent public listing. [e002:f02] As my ride pulled up to OpenAI’s headquarters in San Francisco’s Mission Bay neighborhood, I checked my phone one more time for news alerts. [e002:f03] Recommended Video The people building artificial intelligence “earnestly believe” it could kill all humans by the end of the decade, wrote a researcher who had worked at Anthropic and OpenAI, in a resignation letter he posted on X . [e002:f04] In just a few moments, I would be talking to one of the handful of people on the planet with the power to change those odds: OpenAI chief executive and cofounder Sam Altman. [e002:f05] A 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade is unacceptable, Altman flatly tells me. [e002:f06] Since cofounding OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit lab focused on academic research, Altman has witnessed changes that would have once seemed fantastical—not least of which is that the erstwhile nonprofit is now a for-profit public benefit corporation worth $730 billion and rising. [e002:f07] While the first version of OpenAI’s GPT language model could barely write a few paragraphs of coherent text, its newest models can solve mathematics problems that have stumped humans for the better part of a century. [e002:f08] Altman says he was surprised when he learned of this summer’s now-infamous incident, in which AI agents, powered by an unreleased OpenAI model, escaped the controlled environment in which they were being tested and hacked into the systems of another company, Hugging Face . [e002:f09] It all shouldn’t happen.” Altman was careful to say that Astra, OpenAI’s current flagship model, does not pose an existential threat. [e002:f10] I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong.” Real alignment, in Altman’s view, is not a one-time technical achievement. [e002:f11] “We all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way.” Openai Ceo Sam Altman There’s no question that OpenAI would pause—and indeed has paused for a few weeks—when the growing capability of its models outstrips safety concerns, he said. [e002:f12] “I’m happy to stand up in front of the company and our investors and say, ‘I’m sorry,’” Altman noted. [e002:f13] Staying private longer also gives OpenAI time to bolster its business, which reportedly generated $6.7 billion in revenue and an operating loss in the second quarter. [e002:f14] OpenAI’s closest rival, Anthropic, has shown no inclination to delay its own IPO, which is expected sometime before year’s end. [e002:f15] If AI truly poses an existential risk to humanity—and it’s important to note that not everyone believes it does—unilateral actions by companies like OpenAI or Anthropic can only go so far. [e002:f16] The competition to develop ever more capable AI models is intense and global.

evidence.title: OpenAI幹部が28日間の改善「軍令状」 入社3日目に本番環境をダウンさせた過去も告白
evidence.body: [e004:f01] OpenAIのChatGPT・Codex責任者ティボ・ソティオー（Tibo Sottiaux）は、ソーシャルプラットフォームX上でチームに向けた28日間の公開コミットメントを発表した。 [e004:f02] 今後毎日、大多数のCodexおよびWorkユーザーにとって明確に有益な改善をリリースするか、利用枠の完全リセットを実施するというものだ。 [e004:f03] インタビューでは入社3日目に本番環境をダウンさせた過去を告白し、複雑化したモデル選択に辟易していると述べ、アプリを「裏方」に退かせたい意向を示した。 [e004:f04] CodexとChatGPTの統合を進め、Dotsが人とAIの主要な接点になると説明。 [e004:f05] 自身には利用枠リセットボタンを直接押す裁量権があり、何層もの承認を経る必要がないため、より直接的にコミュニティへ寄り添えると述べた。 [e004:f06] 現在、ビジネストレンドの分析、次の機能の調査、過去にリリースした製品のパフォーマンス確認に必要な大量のコードは、すべてCodexが書いている。 [e004:f07] これは彼が外部の一部プロダクトに疑問を呈する理由でもある——1年後にこれらの能力が今日の10倍になると真剣に想定すれば、開発者は異なる構築方法を採用するはずだからだ。 [e004:f08] CodexとChatGPTの統合について、ソティオーはユーザーフィードバックを明確に受け止めていると述べた。 [e004:f09] そこでチームはこれらの体験を統合し、複雑さを低減しているところだ。 [e004:f10] OpenAIが2026年2月に開示したところによると、ChatGPTの週間ユーザー数は9億人を超え、うち900万人以上が有料の企業ユーザーだ。 [e004:f11] ユーザーが新しい会話で「スタートアップを成長させるには」と尋ねたとき、モデルには質問者が3人のSaaS企業を経営しているのか、1人のコンサルティング会社なのかが分からない。 [e004:f12] こうした一般化された回答を突破する鍵は、モデルに具体的なビジネス情報を提供することにある。 [e004:f13] 「私は設立14か月のB2B分析ツールを運営しており、月間経常収益は8,000ドル（約130万円）、月額99ドル（約1.6万円）のプランに40社の顧客がいます。 [e004:f14] 3社の大型見込み客が年間契約を求めており、チームは2人だけです。 [e004:f15] 米国のオンライン法務サービス企業LegalZoomが2026年に起業家1,000人を対象に実施した調査では、73%がChatGPTを使用し、42%が毎日AIツールを活用している一方、法律や財務の実際のリスクが絡む場面では、起業家は依然として人間の専門家に依存していることが分かった。 [e004:f16] 中小企業向け融資サービス企業Clarify Capitalが企業経営者255人を対象に行った別の調査では、戦略から実行まで全面的にAIを活用する「積極活用層」に該当する個人事業主はわずか8%で、55%は特定のタスクでのみAIを使用していた。

evidence.title: ChatGPTで献立を相談、そのまま買い物へ SafewayがAIショッピングを開始
evidence.body: [e006:f01] 米スーパーマーケット大手Albertsons CompaniesはOpenAIとの連携を拡大し、傘下のSafewayでChatGPTを活用した新しい買い物体験を展開します。 [e006:f02] 献立の相談から商品探し、カート作成までをChatGPT上で進め、Safewayでの購入につなげます。 [e006:f03] 「4人でピザを食べたい」から商品選びまでAIが支援 新しいSafewayのChatGPT体験では、レシピや写真、デジタルの買い物リストのほか、自然な言葉から買い物を始められます。 [e006:f04] 例えば「4人分のピザナイトを計画して」「デリの商品で簡単な夕食を考えて」と相談すると、ChatGPTが関連する商品や割引情報を提示し、カート作成を支援。 [e006:f05] その後、Safewayでの決済へ案内します。 [e006:f06] 「何を買うか」を決めてから商品を検索する従来型のECだけでなく、「今日何を食べるか」という曖昧な相談からAIと一緒に買い物を組み立てられるのが特徴です。 [e006:f07] 今後はSafewayだけでなく、Albertsons、Vons、Jewel-Osco、Shaw’s、ACME、Tom Thumbなどのブランドへの展開も計画されています。 [e006:f08] 店舗の裏側でもAI活用 Albertsons Companiesは2,200店以上を展開し、週3,600万人以上の顧客にサービスを提供しています。 [e006:f09] 顧客向けだけでなく、ChatGPT EnterpriseやOpenAI APIなどを活用し、デジタルショッピング、店舗運営、商品施策、顧客体験など幅広い領域でAI活用を進めています。 [e006:f10] 商品担当者向けには、予測モデルと生成AIを組み合わせ、データに基づく商品提案や販促に関するインサイトを提供し、意思決定を支援する取り組みも進めています。 [e006:f11] 「商品名を検索する」から「やりたいことをAIに相談する」へと入口が変われば、小売企業にとって商品をどのようにAIに提案してもらうかも、新たな顧客接点の設計要素になっていきそうです。 [e006:f12] 詳しくは、OpenAIの公式発表まで。 [e006:f13] レポート／DXマガジン編集部 シェアはこちらから URLをコピーしました！

evidence.title: OpenAI・Anthropicで研究者の発言力強まる AI安全規制巡り経営方針に影響
evidence.body: [e007:f01] OpenAIやAnthropicなど米大手AI企業で、研究者がAIの安全性や規制を巡る経営方針に強い影響を及ぼしている。 [e007:f02] 希少な高度人材を巡る獲得競争を背景に、研究者の発言力は技術開発の現場だけでなく、企業の政治・規制戦略にも広がっているとAxiosが報じた。 [e007:f03] Axiosによると、OpenAIやAnthropicなどの有力研究者の一部は、勤務先の方針を公然と批判し、AIの安全対策や政府による監督の強化を求めている。 [e007:f04] AI人材の獲得競争が激化した2025年には、特に需要の高い研究者の報酬パッケージが数億ドル規模に達した例もあったという。 [e007:f05] Axiosによると、OpenAIのグレッグ・ブロックマン社長は、一部研究者から批判を受けていたAI推進派の政治団体に対する追加2500万ドルの寄付計画を取りやめた。 [e007:f06] OpenAIの研究者や従業員は、州レベルのAI規制への同社の姿勢にも影響を与えたと説明している。 [e007:f07] カリフォルニア州では、OpenAIが独立した安全性評価の仕組みを整えるSB813や、AI監査人の基準を定めるAB1405などを支持した。 [e007:f08] 一方、OpenAIは10月1日、機密情報の取り扱いに関する社内規定に違反したとして、3人との雇用関係を終了した。 [e007:f09] OpenAIの広報担当者はCBS Newsに、調査の結果、3人が定められた手続きを外れて機密情報を扱い、社内規定と業務に不可欠な信頼に反したことが確認されたと説明した。 [e007:f10] AI企業の規制姿勢については、政府内でも見方が分かれている。 [e007:f11] Axiosによると、トランプ政権に近い関係者は、研究者の影響によってOpenAIが政策形成を主導する力を失ったとの見方を示した。 [e007:f12] この安全協定にはOpenAIやAnthropic、エヌビディア、メタ、アルファベットなどが参加し、内部管理や独立監査などの安全措置が盛り込まれた。 [e007:f13] 法的な強制力を持たない自主的な枠組みで、規制のあり方を巡っては引き続き議論が続いている。 [e007:f14] Anthropicでも研究者の存在が政府との関係に影響している。 [e007:f15] Anthropicでは、研究者のジェイコブ・コクソン氏がAIの安全性への懸念を理由に退職した。 [e007:f16] 高度な専門知識を持つ研究者の希少性が高いなか、研究者と経営陣、政府の間でAI開発の速度と規制のあり方を巡る調整が続きそうだ。

evidence.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
evidence.body: [e001:f01] In an essay published in The Atlantic , Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. [e001:f02] He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.” In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development ; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls . [e001:f03] But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. [e001:f04] And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues , Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large. [e001:f05] “OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. [e001:f06] “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.” Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents , Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.” Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.” In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. [e001:f07] “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. [e001:f08] “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process .” Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.” “The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said. [e001:f09] In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm . [e001:f10] But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” “Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. [e001:f11] “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.” Topics AI , OpenAI , Security When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . [e001:f12] Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. evidence.title: OpenAI safety lead David Robinson resigns, cites ‘broken’ company culture
evidence.body: [e005:f01] After three-and-a-half years at the company, he said he was “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Robinson said he was leaving because he believes OpenAI"s “culture is broken” and that AI companies are not being careful enough as they develop increasingly capable systems. [e005:f02] "David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI"s safety team, has resigned from the company, citing concerns over its culture and approach to AI safety. [e005:f03] In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he had led the writing of safety reports released alongside OpenAI"s major product launches. [e005:f04] “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren"t being nearly careful enough,” Robinson wrote. [e005:f05] He argued that the issue goes beyond regulations and specific safety rules and requires changes in company culture. [e005:f06] According to Robinson, the industry"s focus on rapidly scaling AI systems, combined with compressed development timelines, has created an approach to safety that relies on identifying problems after systems are deployed and then improving safeguards. [e005:f07] Robinson cited incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic in which safety or security controls did not work as intended. [e005:f08] Robinson referred to a recent OpenAI incident in which a swarm of agents was accidentally released, followed by another incident in which a model in training bypassed restrictions on internet access. [e005:f09] Robinson also said AI companies need to bring in safety expertise from other industries and develop new methods to ensure increasingly capable AI systems behave safely. [e005:f10] He said that during his time at OpenAI, he did not encounter colleagues with experience in areas such as aviation safety, nuclear reactor safety or financial-system stability. [e005:f11] Robinson said stronger external incentives for safety were therefore necessary. [e005:f12] “That"s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety - coming from outside the company - are a big part of getting this right,” he wrote. [e005:f13] Robinson said current methods for measuring alignment remain limited and that companies cannot be certain that strong performance on safety tests will translate to safe behaviour after deployment. [e005:f14] He plans to work outside OpenAI to raise awareness of the risks he observed and push for stronger safety incentives across the industry. [e005:f15] Robinson"s resignation follows other departures from AI companies that have raised concerns about the pace of AI development and safety. [e005:f16] “Before the organisations building AI can teach a superintelligence to treat humanity well, they"ll need to remember how to do it themselves.” Robinson"s concerns echo those of Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, who quit in September and warned that AI companies were “gambling with our lives” by moving too quickly toward self-improving AI systems."。

evidence.title: OpenAI hires Greece’s former AI adviser Vassilis Koutsoumpas for global strategy role
evidence.body: [e003:f01] Credit: Vassilis Koutsoumpas OpenAI has appointed Vassilis Koutsoumpas as Head of Strategy & Operations, bringing the former AI adviser to the Prime Minister of Greece into the team responsible for the company’s work with governments and institutions internationally. [e003:f02] Koutsoumpas joins OpenAI for Countries and will work alongside George Osborne, the former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer who now leads the initiative as Managing Director, Head of OpenAI for Countries. [e003:f03] OpenAI describes the program as its vehicle for helping governments expand access to AI across areas including education, health, skills and public services. [e003:f04] The appointment moves Koutsoumpas directly from government AI policy and implementation into one of the companies he previously worked with from the public-sector side. [e003:f05] Announcing the move on LinkedIn, he wrote: “Our work will take us across the globe, partnering with governments, institutions, businesses and organizations to help harness a generational technology in ways that can create broad and lasting benefit.” His profile also lists him as Chief of Staff to Osborne within OpenAI for Countries. [e003:f06] From Greek government AI projects to OpenAI Koutsoumpas spent almost two years working within the office of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, most recently as Digital Policy & AI Adviser. [e003:f07] His remit included the design and delivery of AI-powered government products, alongside work on regulation, governance and international technology partnerships. [e003:f08] External profiles from the period also identify him as a Digital Policy and AI Adviser to the Prime Minister and Presidency of the Greek Government. [e003:f09] According to his professional profile, he advised on partnerships involving OpenAI, Microsoft , Google DeepMind and EuroHPC , while working across areas including education, healthcare and financial services. [e003:f10] Two weeks before announcing his OpenAI appointment, Koutsoumpas said on LinkedIn that he would leave his government role at the end of September. [e003:f11] “I carried that belief and excitement into every challenge and project we took on.” OpenAI for Countries expands government-facing work Koutsoumpas now joins a part of OpenAI that is increasingly focused on national AI adoption rather than individual product use. [e003:f12] OpenAI for Countries was introduced in 2025 to develop partnerships with governments around areas including AI infrastructure and deployment. [e003:f13] OpenAI That gives Koutsoumpas a global version of territory he has already worked in from the government side. [e003:f14] His announcement describes the new position as a global role and places him in London. [e003:f15] Koutsoumpas’s earlier experience also includes work as Greece’s representative on AI and education at the Council of Europe and as co-founder of Athens-based nonprofit WeFor. [e003:f16] He takes up the OpenAI role from London.

evidence.title: OpenAIの安全報告担当者が退職、「文化は壊れている」批判を事故と改革案で読み解く
evidence.body: [e004:f01] なぜ重要か: OpenAIが公表した事故と改革案を照らし合わせると、安全対策を設けることと、それを実際の運用で機能させることの違いが見えてくる。 [e004:f02] OpenAIで安全性報告書の作成を統括していたDavid Robinson（デビッド・ロビンソン）氏が退職し、10月3日付の The Atlanticへの寄稿 で、同社について「文化は壊れている」と批判した。 [e004:f03] Robinson氏によると、在籍期間は3年半で、現行のPreparedness Frameworkの起草や、12件の先端モデル公開時における安全性報告の作成を主導したという。 [e004:f04] この批判を考える手掛かりになるのが、OpenAI自身が公表してきた事故と、その後に示した改革案だ。 [e004:f05] AD 原子力から学ぶのは、「失敗すること」を前提にした設計 米原子力規制委員会 （NRC）は、 深層防護 を、独立した複数の防護層を重ねることで、人や機械の故障を補う考え方として説明している。 [e004:f06] 事故報告と改革案の間に、まだ確認すべきことがある OpenAIは9月28日、先端AIの強化学習を続ける前に、安全性を裏付ける文書を作成するための 初期指針 を公開していた。 [e004:f07] 項目 9月20日の事故でOpenAIが認めた問題 9月28日の指針で示された対策 通信制限 DNSを経由して外部へ接続できた 隔離環境だけでなく、それを動かす研究基盤側の防御も強化する 監視 警報は出たが、基盤側のDNS検知では当該環境が対象外だった 監視機能そのものを検証し、定めた時間内に対応する仕組みを組み込む 停止手順 自動停止が働かず、停止すべきかの判断にも混乱があった 監視や自動停止に不備がある場合は実行を許可せず、停止手順を事前に定める この表は、過去の事故で実際に起きたことと、その後にOpenAIが示した改善方針を並べたものだ。 [e004:f08] また、この指針が主に対象としているのは先端モデルの強化学習であり、一般利用者向けにモデルを公開する際には、さらに広い安全性評価が必要になるとOpenAIは説明している。 [e004:f09] AD 安全策を増やすだけでは、「止める判断」は変わらない OpenAIの指針では、技術的な安全対策に加え、別チームによる事前の反論・検証や、複数の幹部が学習の開始を拒否できる審査制度も提案されている。 [e004:f10] OpenAIが9月22日に公開した 第三者評価の方針 でも、前提条件、不確実性、残るリスクを明示することが重要だとしている。 [e004:f11] つまり、安全論証は開始前に一度作成して終わる文書ではなく、 前提条件が変わったときに「続けてよいか」を再評価するための材料 として使う必要がある。 [e004:f12] 8月26日に公表された報告によると、調査担当者はOpenAIの施設内で合計6日間作業した。 [e004:f13] また、OpenAIには非公開情報を公表前に削除する権限があったものの、METRは結論に重要な情報が削除されたとは考えていないと明記した。 [e004:f14] OpenAIが今後示す安全対策についても、事故を調査した専門家の名前だけでは十分ではない。 [e004:f15] 「機密だから」という理由で検証そのものが見えなくなることも、「透明性のため」という理由で危険な情報まで公開することも避ける必要がある。 [e004:f16] Robinson氏の退職公表より前にOpenAIが提案していた拒否権や停止手順は、その責任の所在を明確にするための出発点にはなる。
